In summary, our research is concerned with
the biogeography of extinct birds, the effects of prehistoric people on island faunas, and the evolution of island faunas.
the effects of human activities on the biota of the tropical Pacific.
the biogeography of Pacific parrots and with the effects of human impact on avifaunas in general.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the extinction of E. roratu infectus is the 18th example of a human-caused extinction of an eastern Oceania land bird.
the extinction of the parrots of the Pacific Islands is due to human impact.
human activities have eliminated all the easternmost species of land birds in at least 18 genera in Oceania (excluding New Zealand and Hawaii).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the parrot genus Eclectus is extinct in Tonga and Vanatu, and probably in Fiji, but is extant on islands to the west.
human impact on the avifaunas of Oceania is extensive and that it is likely to continue to have significant effects on the region's biota.
the human colonization of the Pacific islands has had an impact on avifaunas that is unparalleled elsewhere.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the parrots of Tonga were not the only ones to disappear in human times.

the human-caused extirpations of birds in the Pacific Islands have been more severe than previously thought, and this is a pattern seen throughout the world, with humans having caused the extinction of at least 1,300 bird species in the past 500 yr.
the parrot genus Eclectus is a good example of the general principle that the extinction of the last member of an island species assemblage can occur rapidly after the arrival of humans.
